# Copper May 2010 

- During May European debt woes took centre stage with the copper market reacting in three distinct phases over the course of the month.  Initially, between the 4th and the 12th price volatility was much in evidence as nervous trading conditions saw 3m quotes oscillating above and below the $7000/t mark.  Then, the real panic set in which resulted in 3m copper falling by more than $620/t over five consecutive trading days before establishing a base at $6502/t on the 19th.  Since then, prices have rallied, cancelling out much of the earlier losses with 3m quotes trading at $7050/t at the time of writing. 

- Recent official consumption data releases for Q1 indicate that demand in some countries and particularly in Japan was much stronger than we had anticipated.  We now estimate that supply exceeded demand by ~280kt in Q1 compared with our previous forecast of ~350kt.  In general, consumption through Q2 has continued to hold up well, largely reflecting restocking, while refined production has underperformed.  As a consequence, we have increased our global market deficit for the quarter, lifting it from ~240kt previously to ~255kt. 

- Following various conversations with market participants it is clear that there are still concerns over the prospects for global consumption performance during H2.  Thus far in 2010 the recovery in demand outside of China has been led by inventory adjustments and by government stimulus packages, many of which are coming to an end.  Meanwhile the construction malaise persists in most developed economies and even when these markets recover the lagged nature of copper usage in construction means that a marked pick up in demand is still some way off. 

- There was only one spot concentrate tender of note during May with miners preferring to sell material to the trade on a more private basis.  Chinese smelters have backed away from the spot market and, barring one or two producers, bids have been far less aggressive of late.  That said spot concentrate headline numbers remain at last month’s levels of $5-10/t & 0.5-1.0c/lb.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Mixed trading patterns during May** During

May European debt woes took centre stage with the copper market reacting in three distinct phases over the course of the month.  Initially, between the 4<sup>th</sup> and the 12<sup>th</sup> price volatility was much in evidence as nervous trading conditions saw 3m quotes oscillating above and below the $7000/t mark.  Then, the real panic set in, leading to an across-the-board sell off in commodities (including gold) in response to market participants reweighting their portfolios towards lower risk investments.  As a consequence 3m copper fell by more than $620/t over the next five trading days before establishing a base at $6502/t on the 19<sup>th</sup> .  Since then, prices have rallied, cancelling out much of the earlier losses with 3m quotes trading at $7050/t at the time of writing **.** 

**Investors deleverage during May** With the events of late 2008/early 2009 still very much in the minds of investors the spectre of sovereign debt defaults within the Eurozone potentially sparking off another banking crisis and a double-dip recession clearly sent a chill through the markets this month.  Little surprise then that investors acted quickly to deleverage and channel funds into the safe harbour provided by the US dollar and US treasury bills.  This resulted in the dollar appreciating against most of the world’s currencies and saw yields on two year treasury bonds fall to an all-time low.  Interestingly, the plunge in commodities prices occurred after the EU-IMF bailout package for Greece was announced.  Not helping matters also was the introduction by the German government of a temporary ban on the naked short selling of equities and European bonds using credit default swaps.  The subsequent price rally occurred on the back of dollar weakness and rising US equities.  Indeed confidence continued to grow over the balance of the month only to be dented, albeit briefly, by sabre rattling between North and South Korea.  Also boosting market sentiment towards month-end was the news from the Chinese official Xinhua News Agency that the country’s sovereign wealth fund was committed to maintaining its euro investments.  As of the 27<sup>th</sup> , official 3-month quotes averaged $6868/t.  This was down 11.7% from April’s average of $7779/t and represented the largest monthly decline since December 2008. 

**Investor interest in commodities may be changing** This month’s deleveraging and flight to safety comes against a backdrop which implies that investor interest in commodities, at least as far as the use of index type products, may be changing. The latest data from the US Commodities Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) suggested that the pace of inflows into commodity index type products slowed during the first quarter.  According to the CFTC, the total notional value of long positions was $215.9Bn at the end of March compared with $211.2Bn at the end of 2009, the value of short positions was $54.7Bn up from $51.3Bn.  As a result, the net long positio

n of $161.2Bn was less than 1% higher than at the end of 2009 with the bulk of the growth coming from positions held on non-US markets. In terms of metals, the CFTC only breaks out data relating to copper which showed that the value of long positions at the end of March was $7.3Bn, down from $8.2Bn at the end of 2009 and the value of short positions was unchanged at $1.8Bn, with the net long position thus totalling $5.5Bn, a decline of 14%. In terms of copper equivalent futures contracts, the size of long positions declined from 98k at the end of 2009 to 82k at the end of March, while the size of short positions declined from 22k to 19k contracts. Given that copper prices climbed by 7% between the end of 2009 and the end of the first quarter, the 14% reduction in the net long position suggests that that there was an outflow of investor funds from copper during the first quarter. The change also decreased the proportion of long to short positions from 4.6:1 to 4.1:1, a more significant shift than that seen for commodities indexes as a whole which saw the ratio of long to short positions shift from 4.1:1 to 3.9:1. If similar patterns have developed in the other non-ferrous metals components of commodity indexes, most notably aluminium and zinc, the combination of lower numbers of futures contracts being rolled forward, together with a relative increase in the short positions may well have been a contributory factor to the general weakness in metals prices across the base metals complex thus far in 2010. #### **Copper LME open interest vs copper price** 300000 8000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - May 2010 Page 2 of 25 Copper Monthly Update **Long liquidation during May** The downgrading of speculative interest during the month was further highlighted by recent LME open interest data which continued to indicate similar trends as were seen in late April, with long liquidation driving falling prices. With a significant number of copper long positions having been established this year, recent economic events would have provided compelling reasons for market participants to lock in profits by closing out their longs. The copper data is not as bearish in comparison with lead or zinc, for example, where heavy shorting has occurred. Indeed, with prices having approached 2010 lows, scope for further long liquidation is much more limited. **Exchange stocks decrease** Total exchange stocks decreased by a net 51.5kt during May to 726.6kt, their lowest level thus far this year. In terms of days of consumption, total exchange inventories were equivalent to 14.5 days, down from 15.5 days in April. The decline reflected

net withdrawals on LME and SHFE exchanges while Comex warehouses were relatively unchanged at 92.2kt.  In China, SHFE inventories dropped by a net 31.7kt to 157.7kt, their largest monthly decline since May 2004, while LME stocks fell by a net 20.3kt to 476.7kt.  The reduction in LME warrants represented the third consecutive month of decline and had been expected in light of the level of last month’s cancelled warrants, that totalled 24.1kt.  The largest withdrawals occurred in the US where inventories fell by a net 11.4kt to 316.8kt.  This mainly reflected deliveries (-11.6kt) out of warehouses in New Orleans.  Elsewhere, European stocks fell by a net 2.5kt, to 62.8kt, while inventories in South Korea and Singapore declined by a net 2.1kt and 3.5kt respectively.  Withdrawals from the latter two locations were most likely material being shipped to China because of improved arbitrage conditions.  At the time of writing (the 28<sup>th</sup> ), LME cancelled warrants totalled 22.7kt, suggesting that further withdrawals will take place in the coming weeks. 

**European premia remain firm** European premia remained firm during the month on the back of the ongoing decline in European LME inventories.  As of the 27<sup>th</sup> European LME inventories stood at 63kt, or just 8.2 days of consumption and only 13% of total LME warrants.  Europe’s share of overall LME inventories has declined since the start of last year with these warehouses holding 48% of total LME stocks.  During the month premia were also supported by the weaker price environment which encouraged some consumers back into the market place.  Chilean and grade A cathode form Rotterdam continued to fetch $80/t while Italian warrants traded slightly higher at $85/t.  Elsewhere, standard grade material remained $20/t above LME. 

**US premia unchanged** US premia continued to trade between 4-4.5c/lb in May amid relatively quiet spot market conditions.  A rise to 5c/lb during the latter stages of last month was the result of tighter scrap availability.  However, Chinese demand for US scrap has eased in recent weeks because of rising copper prices which is also reflected in lower cathode premia.  Despite this, we understand that some scrap traders are holding material back from the market awaiting even higher prices.  There is thus the potential for cathode premia to strengthen in the coming weeks if sufficient scrap material is held back from the market place (or if Xstrata’s CCR refinery workers go on strike on May 31<sup>st</sup> ). 

**Chinese premia weaken** Chinese premia weakened during the first week of the month having fallen from $80/t at the end of April to $60/t.  The decline occurred in tandem with falling physical demand and unfavourable arbitrage conditions. Falling LME prices also saw consumers stay out of the market because they wanted to see if prices would fall further. However, a change in arbitrage conditions during the second half of May resulted in increased demand for sp

ot material. Spot premia have thus strengthened again and are currently trading between $70-90/t. #### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

**Shanghai arbitrage conditions improve** The more favourable SHFE/LME arbitrage conditions arose on account of the sharp decline in LME prices that also fell below SHFE quotes. As of the 27th the LME traded below SHFE by an average Metals Market Service Monthly Update - May 2010 Page 3 of 25 Copper Monthly Update of $67/t (exclusive of VAT). This compared with the LME trading above SHFE prices by an average of $147/t in April and $14/t in March. As a consequence of these favourable arbitrage conditions this month, all other things being equal we would expect to see a rise in refined imports over the next four to six weeks (this being the normal lead time between metal being booked and when it arrives in China, unless material is shipped directly from Chinese bonded warehouses). **Chinese refined imports fall in April from a year earlier** According to latest Chinese trade data the country’s refined imports fell by 2.6% in April from a year earlier. On a month-on-month basis imports were down by a greater 8.1% from March. This was not surprising due to less favourable arbitrage opportunities during March. This downward trend is likely to have continued through May in lieu of the negative arbitrage opportunities in April. However, as noted previously, imports could improve again in June. This will be driven by the opening up of the arbitrage during May as well as reduced imports of scrap following the implementation of the new copper scrap import policy on June 1st . **Scrap imports may slow in the coming months** China’s General Administration of Customs announced in April that a new scrap policy will be introduced on June 1st aimed at preventing tax evasion by importers. The new scheme will require scrap importers to clearly declare the metal content of their imports for checking by more rigorous custom inspections in designated places at port sides. This should help to eliminate the previous practice of understating the copper content of imported scrap in order to reduce the amount of VAT (17%) payable. The new legislation will result in closer scrutiny of the shipments by custom departments which could lead to higher costs for importers and, in turn, reduced imports. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 Refined Imports 400

**Q1 demand strong** Recent official consumption data releases for Q1 indicate that demand in some countries and particularly in Japan was much stronger than we had anticipated (see consumption). We now estimate that supply exceeded demand by ~280kt in Q1 compared with our previous forecast of ~350kt. In general, consumption through Q2 has continued to hold up well, largely reflecting restocking, while refined production has underperformed. As a consequence, we have increased our global market deficit for the quarter, lifting it from ~240kt previously to ~255kt. However, we have lowered our average price forecast for Q2, down from $7500/t in April to $7150/t, to reflect the current weaker price environment. Following various conversations with market participants it is clear that there are still concerns over the prospects for global consumption performance during H2. Thus far in 2010 the recovery in demand outside of China has been led by inventory adjustments and by government stimulus packages, many of which are coming to an end. Meanwhile the construction malaise persists in most developed economies and even when these markets recover the lagged nature of copper usage in construction means that a marked pick up in demand is still some way off. At the same time, Chinese copper consumption growth continues at exceedingly high levels with output of semis through April having increased by almost 22% year on year according to CNIA data. It is difficult to envisage this rate being sustained over the balance of the year particularly in light of the focus on cooling certain sectors of the Chinese economy at present. Thus we forecast slower overall growth in H2 2010 with the global market in surplus throughout this period and with prices trending down. For 2010 we forecast a market surplus of ~245kt and average prices increasing by 36.3% to $7048/t ($3.20/lb). This is down from our previous estimate of $7160/t (3.25c/lb). **Full demand recovery expected in 2011** In 2011 a full recovery in underlying demand is expected, alongside improving construction activity, with global refined consumption forecast to rise by 6.3% to ~19.4Mt. Marginal supply growth should see global refined production increasing by 0.9% to ~19.4Mt, resulting in a balanced market. Despite this, prices are forecast to fall moderately, by 3.2% to an average of $6825/t ($3.10/lb) due to our expectation of an anticipated and ongoing “investment portfolio bleed out” (discussed in last month’s report). Metals Market Service Monthly Update - May 2010 Page 5 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Technical Analysis Copper collapsed over early May making a closing low of $6,470/t on the 17th . Prices have subsequently moved up towards key support/resistance at $6,900/t. A pick up in volume at the recent lows provides some comfort with long-term momentum measure neutral. Prices are likely to continue to move in the direction of economic sentiment rather than copper market fundamentals whilst the wider financial uncertainty continues. On the upside resistance can be expected at $6,900/t, $7,200/t and $8,000/t, close to the April highs. A break through $8,000/t targeting $8,800/t is unlikely to arise over June. On the downside support is anticipated at the recent closing low of $6,470/t and then at retracement levels $6,000/t and $5,400/t. Further support is expected at February’s closing low of $6,280/t. Industrial output increased by 1% in April from March, and over the past three months has risen at an annual rate 8.3%. In April, the headline index rose above 60 for the first time since 2004, with output and new orders accelerating. In addition, a wider gap between the new orders and inventories indices is a good indication that a further inventory-based boost to production is likely. #### **US industrial production and manufacturing PMI** 10% 65

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - May 2010 Page 7 of 25 Copper Monthly Update **US consumer remains critical to sustained recovery** Retail sales data suggest consumers are starting to spend once again at a healthy rate. Spending in April increased by 8.8% year on year, and on a levels basis is now within 3.6% of the pre-crisis peak. Over the past three months, retail sales have grown at an annualised rate of 12.6%. Although a significant part of the increase in sales is likely coming from pent up demand, some of the increased spending may be due to an improvement in the US employment situation. Nonfarm employment increased by 290,000 in April, following on from the 230,000 gain in March, thanks to a surge in private employment. The data also showed that average hours worked per week continued to improve. Notably, nearly every major industry added to payrolls, suggesting that jobs growth is both broad and more durable. However, we are conscious that the rise in U

S consumer spending has been from a low base, and overall we still expect the US consumer to be relatively weak through 2010. **Business investment also needs to improve** There are now strong signs that business investment is improving. New orders for durable goods increased by 2.9% month-on-month in April and core capital goods orders (excluding the volatile aircraft sector) have been rising sharply, at an average rate of 2.4% month on month in the past three months, and are up by 15% year on year for the first four months of 2010. However, it is worth noting that durable goods orders collapsed by 24% from their peak through to June 2009, so have some distance yet to go (~17%) to get back to precrisis levels. **Higher lending rates pose risk to recovery** A key risk facing the recovery in business spending and the wider US recovery originates from the eurozone debt crisis and the associated increase in LIBOR. A perceived deterioration in the global banking sector, stemming from the European sovereign debt crisis, has driven interbank lending rates higher. The chart below illustrates a rapid increase in the spread between interbank lending rates and the yield on a 3-month US T- Bill. While this spread remains well below the levels reached around the time of the Lehman collapse, this widening in spread effectively increases the premium that businesses have to pay to borrow, thus pushing up the cost of investing in new capital. Tightening financial market conditions are not yet derailing the recovery, but they do pose a downside risk that must be monitored closely. #### **Spread between 3-month US$ LIBOR and 3-month US T-bill yield** 0.45

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - May 2010 Page 8 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Consumption **Final numbers for 2009 continue to be reported** We have made a few amendments to our demand forecasts since our last monthly report to reflect official reported data for Q1. The reported data showed that demand in Japan during the first three months of the year was much stronger than we had originally anticipated and resulted in us lifting our Japanese forecast for this year by ~50kt to ~1Mt. Likewise in Italy, stronger than expected growth in Q1 resulted in us lifting our Italian demand forecast by 12kt to ~550kt. However, these net gains were partly offset by weaker than expected demand in France, South Africa and Romania. As a consequence of all the revisions we have raised our 2010 demand estimate by a net 35kt and now estimate that global refined copper consumption will increase by 5.9% this year to ~18.3Mt. The knock-on effect of these revisions is to increase our 2011 and 2012 demand forecasts by 13kt and 34kt to 19.4Mt and 20.2Mt res

pectively, representing annual growth rates of 6.3% and 3.9%. ### **Japan** **Strong recovery in demand for copper and copper alloy products during Q1** Demand for copper and copper alloy products continued to recover during March. According to the Japan Copper and Brass Manufacturers Association, output of copper semi products increased by 120.4% from a year earlier. This represented the fifth consecutive month of annual increase as well as the largest annual percentage gain since the association started to collect monthly data in January 1953. The large gain partly reflected growth coming from a low base, where production in March 2009 fell by 60% from a year earlier, as well as increased export demand. The sharp gain in March meant that the production of copper and copper alloy products increased by 88.2% overall in Q1 from the corresponding period in 2009. **Demand for copper and copper alloy strip drive recovery** Demand for copper strip was particularly strong during Q1 where the Japan Copper and Brass Manufacturers Association reported a 215.5% (+45kt) annual jump in production. Supporting this growth was increased export orders which mainly reflected robust Chinese demand for digital home electronics. Buoyant demand from Japan’s domestic semi conductor and automotive sectors also helped support the gain. According to latest government statistics Japanese vehicle output continued to recover strongly in March where production increased by 71% from a year earlier to its highest level since November 2008. For the first three months of the year production surged 57.8% year on year. The healthy growth in auto production also helped support rising orders for brass strip where output increased by 260% (+21.4kt) during the first three months of the year from the corresponding period in 2009. In March production of brass strip exceeded 10kt for the first time since October 2008. Also positive was the production of bronze sheet and strip which increased by 262% (+9kt) year on year during Q1. According to the Japan Cable Makers Association shipments to these two sectors increased by 78% and 68% respectively in March from a year earlier. For Q1 as a whole deliveries to these sectors increased by 62% and 52% respectively. Elsewhere in the other wire and cable markets the recovery in demand was less strong which is reflected in total wire and cable shipments increasing by 8.4% year on year in Q1. The lower rate largely reflected ongoing weakness in the construction sector where deliveries to this sector declined by 10.8% during the first three months of the year from the corresponding period in 2009, according to the Japan Cable Makers association. As yet there has been no significant recovery in the construction sector where housing starts fell by 2.4% year on year in March and 6.6% for Q1 as a whole from a year earlier. Any sustained recovery in housing starts is being hampered by wage deflation and unemployment. **Japan’s emphatic pace of demand recovery not expected to be maintained throughout the year** Latest data from the Japan Cable Makers Association showed that shipments increased by a further 14.8% in April from a year earlier. Once again the gain was driven by strong demand from the auto and electrical and electronic sectors. However, this rate of growth is not expected to be maintained throughout the remainder of the year. There is concern that once the auto ‘eco-scrapping’ scheme comes to an end in September there will be a sharp fall in auto production. Meanwhile the healthy growth in demand for electrical and electronic products partly reflects restocking which, when this comes to an end, will result in demand weakening unless there is fresh underlying demand to take up the slack. However, there is concern that Japan’s economy will be very slow to recover fully in light of deflation and ongoing unemployment. With this in mind we forecast that Japanese refined copper consumption will increase by 8.5% this year to 950kt. Previously we were forecasting annual growth of 3% to just over 900kt. ### **Europe** **European demand recovered strongly during Q1** The strength of the recovery in European copper demand during Q1 was highlighted recently by positive comments from two of the region’s main copper semi producers, Aurubis and KME, and Assomet, Italy’s non ferrous n

ational association.  Aurubis reported that production of copper wire rod from its plants in Germany and Italy increased by a combined 16% in Q1, to 195kt, from a year earlier.  This represented the highest level since Q2 2008.  While the company reported healthy demand from most of the wire and cable markets, orders for enamelled and automotive wire were particularly strong.  The former reflected increased export orders of white goods, alongside the weaker euro, while the latter reflected increased auto production.  According to J.D Power Western European auto production increased by 27.8% in Q1 from the corresponding period in 2009.  The company’s increase in wire rod production was also supported by ongoing investment within the energy sector despite some infrastructure projects being delayed because of the severe winter.  One other factor reflecting Aurubis’s positive result was increased market share following the closure of Nexan’s Chauny wire rod plant in France last year. 

**Demand for copper semi products also positive** Aurubis also reported positive demand for its copper shapes during Q1 where production increased by 55% year on year to 36kt.  Similar to its wire rod output, this represented the highest level since Q2 2008.  Strong orders from the electrical and electronic and automotive sectors were largely responsible for the growth.  Another contributing factor was a stronger dollar which encouraged the exports of semi-finished products to North America and the Far East. 

**KME and Assomet report positive results** Europe’s buoyant auto sector was also responsible for both KME and Assomet reporting positive production results during Q1.  KME, who has copper semi manufacturing plants in Germany, Italy, France, UK and Spain, reported a 10.5% (+12kt) increase in its output of copper and copper alloy products in Q1 from a year earlier.  Fortunately robust orders from the auto sector and domestic appliance manufacturers helped offset weak demand from Europe’s construction sector.  According to KME several construction projects during Q1 were postponed because of bad weather in both Europe and North America.  Meanwhile in Italy, Assomet reported that the production of copper and copper alloy products increased by 19.8% year on year in Q1 to 290kt.  According to the association the output of copper semi products increased by 10%, to 150kt, during the three-month period from a year earlier while the production of copper alloy products jumped annually by 32.5% to 140kt.  In both cases this represented their highest output rate since Q2 2008.  The gain reflected healthy demand from the auto sector as well as improving orders from the manufacturers of components which are consumed by the power generation and renewable energy industries. 

**European demand expected to slow during H2** Despite the positive production results reported for Q1 there is concern that this momentum will not be maintained during H2, as we noted in our previous month

ly report.  There is little evidence to suggest that the recovery in orders reflected any significant improvement in end-use demand.  Our sources informed us that the pick up was largely due to restocking because of lean pipeline supplies.  Therefore, once the inventory adjustment is complete demand will fall off unless there is a significant improvement in underlying demand. Indeed a small drop has already been witnessed in the auto sector, one of the main drivers of demand thus far this year, where European auto production fell by 7.7% in April from March.  On an annual basis output increased by 8.5% but this was significantly below the annual average of 28.4% recorded during Q1.  Overall we forecast that European refined copper consumption will increase by 1.8% this year to just below 2.8Mt.  However, the majority of this growth is expected to occur during the first six months of the year where demand will increase by 3.4% year on year to just over 1.3Mt. During H2 demand is expected to be equal to last year at ~1.4Mt.

**First Quantum’s DRC assets awarded to SODIMICO** Sociйtй de Dйveloppement Industriel et Minier du Congo (SODIMICO) has brought a case against the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) requesting the annulment of a letter written by a former DRC Minister of Mines dated February 2000 pursuant to which the DRC allegedly withdrew exploration rights belonging to SODIMICO.  As a consequ

ence, SODIMICO requested its rights be reinstated on the exclusive exploration zones which SODIMICO previously held which were allegedly converted into a number of exploration and exploitation licences now held by First Quantum Minerals (FQM) through its subsidiaries Frontier SPRL and Comisa SPRL, operators of the Frontier and Lonshi mines.  A hearing was held on May 14th 2010 where the DRC Supreme Court rejected all arguments submitted by Frontier and Comisa with the court cancelling the Minister of Mines February 2000 letter and reassigning the mining rights and titles to SODIMICO.  To date FQM has reported that no direct action has been taken by the DRC authorities against either Frontier or Lonshi as a result of the Supreme Court decision and these mines continue to operate normally.  The company has also stated that it is extremely concerned with the orchestrated attack on the Frontier and Lonshi operations in what it says is obvious retaliation for its commencement of international arbitration with respect to the illegal cancellation of its Kolwezi Project and FQM’s refusal to resolve this dispute by agreeing to submit to arrangements with unspecified third parties.  The company has thus far invested $750M in the Kolwezi Project and over $300M at Frontier on the basis of mining licences granted under the World Bank sponsored Mining Code, having obtained all necessary government approvals and permits.  The 92kt/a Frontier mine recently made a tax payment of $55M which is the largest ever in the DRC. 

**Tia Maria desalination plant may be viable** Last month the Peruvian Government ordered Southern Copper to stop construction work on its $1Bn Tia Maria project for three months following protests against the project by residents in the south of Arequipa (the main fear of local residents being the affect that the mine will have on their water reserves). According to the Peruvian Mines and Energy minister a desalination plant appeared to be the only way in which approval would be granted to continue developing the project.  Although Southern Copper had all but ruled out building a desalination plant, in late May the company’s CEO stated that this option appeared to be viable. 

**Yunnan Copper to commission new refinery in July** Yunnan Copper is to commission its new 100kt/a Qingyuan tank house in Guangdong province on July 1<sup>st</sup> .  Initially, the refinery will source blister copper from Yunnan’s part-owned Chambishi smelter in Zambia (Yunnan currently refines a proportion of this material through its Kunming plant, both through direct contracts and also via traders).  The company is aiming eventually to initiate stage II and stage III expansions that will raise the overall capacity to 400kt/a.  Stage II will focus on scrap sources and there may also be plans under phase III to add a primary smelter (200kt/a) to handle concentrates form Chinalco’s Toromocho project. 

**Ivanhoe looks for initial funding for Oyu Tolgoi** Ivanhoe Mines

has signed a joint mandate letter with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (ERBD) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC) for evaluation of a major financing package for the construction of the planned Oyu Tolgoi mining complex in southern Mongolia. Under the terms of the letter, the EBRD and the World Bank Group’s IFC will consider providing a two-part package consisting of up to $300M each from the EBRD and IFC, as part of a group of primary lenders, in limited-recourse project financing and the mobilisation of a further $1.2Bn from commercial lenders under a “B loan” structure. Ivanhoe Mines also has received expressions of interest from export credit agencies to provide up to $500M in direct project debt financing. Ivanhoe and Rio Tinto have a stated objective of commencing commercial production at Oyu Tolgoi in 2013. The recently released 2010 Oyu Tolgoi Integrated Development Plan estimated that the initial capital cost required to achieve first production from the open-pit mine on the Southern Oyu deposits is $4.6Bn. This amount includes $1.1Bn to be spent advancing underground development at the Hugo North Deposit in preparation for the start of block-cave mining following the start of production from the open pit. Options to finance the remainder of the estimated capital cost include, but are not limited to, additional potential debt, equity offerings, a credit facility, the sale of subsidiaries, equity investments, project financing and/or various corporate transactions. In a separate development Ivanhoe Australia has agreed to purchase the Osborne mine in Queensland from Barrick Australia for $27M. The Osborne ore reserves are now virtually depleted but the acquisition of the milling facilities will help Ivanhoe to fast track developing various molybdenum/rhenium deposits in the Cloncurry district. The company will also examine the potential for operating separate mill lines to process copper-gold ore deposits in the region.
